Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: The night his seven-year-old son collapsed with a sudden, raging fever and respiratory distress, Minh’s world fractured into sharp, unblinking frames. He had been driving forty minutes from his Iowa cornfields to the county hospital when the emergency line connected. By the time he burst into the pediatric ICU, his son’s small body was fighting for air. Minh memorized the specific angles of his son’s life-threatening state: the taut, pale skin stretched over the ribs that heaved with every shallow breath, the bruised, swollen wrist where the trauma nurse had struggled to secure an IV line, and the way his son’s lips had turned a frightening, chalky blue. In the waiting room, a radio played a familiar acoustic track that his son had hummed all summer. That specific song, along with the sight of his son’s chest and the bruised wrist, became anchored to the night his child nearly slipped away. Now, hearing a similar melody on the feed store radio or from a passing car drags him right back to that sterile hallway. In the weeks that followed, the medical crisis refused to recede into the past. When Minh closed his eyes or found himself alone in the barn, the frightening event did not unfold as a recollection; it arrived fully formed, as though he were standing over that hospital bed again. He was certain that the illness had not finished its work, that the danger was still hovering in the room. Fragments of the night would suddenly appear without warning—a flash of the IV tape, a memory of the monitor’s steady beep, the sight of his son’s flared nostrils—and then vanish just as quickly, leaving him breathless and disoriented. What frightened him most was the certainty that his son could vanish at any moment, that the fragile health they had fought for was still a glass house. The memory did not feel like something that had ended; it felt like it was happening right now, demanding a response that his living room or tractor cabin could not provide. The days began to stretch into a quiet, parallel routine. Minh stayed up until very late, pacing the kitchen or watching the security cameras monitor the back pasture. Going to sleep or lying in the dark made his breath catch, so he simply delayed it, hour after hour, until exhaustion pulled him under. During daylight, he walked the same perimeter of his property, deliberately taking long detours around town to skip the grocery store, the hardware shop, and the other parents at the school drop-off. Avoiding people settled over him like a second skin. He stopped attending community gatherings and let his wife manage the children’s calls. The farm, once a place of steady rhythm, became a solitary stretch of fenced fields. His boots tracked mud through the same rows, his hands grew calloused from pulling weeds and repairing fence lines, while the house grew quieter. He had left the Central Highlands of Vietnam decades ago to build this land, but now the soil felt like shifting sand beneath his boots. Now, at forty-two, Minh’s marriage has grown quiet, and the crops yield less as his attention fractures under the weight of constant vigilance. The turning point came three weeks ago when he woke in the dark of his bedroom, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he was back in the ICU waiting room. He stumbled out to the porch, unable to move, and for the first time in months, he broke down weeping in front of his wife. He had come to believe that staying awake was the only way to keep the past at bay, but the exhaustion was making him dangerous around heavy machinery and the livestock. He finally stepped into the clinic with a list of his symptoms, hoping the therapists might offer him a way to let his son be just a boy again, and to let his own mind rest through the night without the constant, suffocating fear that the darkness would swallow him whole.
